summary: The note describes how ergonomically designed sports equipment is increasingly used to reduce injuries and extend athletic careers, not just boost performance. It profiles designers, consultants, advocates and athletes such as Joseph Kimani, Alicia Hartfield and Mark Schultz who returned from injury with custom gear. It also highlights 3D scanning and printing as making personalization more accessible, and looks to a future where gear is a partner in health and performance.
one_line: Ergonomic, increasingly customized sports gear is cutting injuries and helping athletes recover, return, and extend their careers across many sports.
key_facts: Since September 1, 2023, collaboration among sports scientists, engineers and professional athletes on customized equipment has surged.
Steve Clarkson, a biomechanist working with collegiate football players, partnered with a leading sports equipment manufacturer to create a bespoke football helmet designed to reduce concussion risk.
Sarah Torres, a former Olympic cyclist turned product designer, developed bicycles that align with riders' natural posture while reducing drag, which she calls "game-changing".
In October 2024, long-distance runner Joseph Kimani suffered a knee injury that kept him out for over six months.
After Joseph Kimani was fitted with custom-designed running shoes that distributed impact more evenly, he returned to competition and shattered his personal best.
Gymnast Alicia Hartfield, who had persistent wrist strains, switched to ergonomically enhanced hand grips, trained harder and went on to claim titles.
Jack Philips, an ergonomics consultant specializing in sports gear, says designing equipment that conforms to athletes' anatomy and movement helps "unlock the athlete's full potential."
Jack Philips and his team designed ergonomic basketball footwear that absorbs shock and minimizes stress on the ankles and knees.
3D scanning and printing allow gear to be tailored to athletes' physiological measurements and performance metrics, once a privilege of the elite but becoming more accessible.
Swimmer Mark Schultz returned after a shoulder injury in late 2023 with a custom-fitted swimsuit and goggles, and credited them with helping him swim pain-free.
Dr. Lila Rodriguez, a sports physician, advocates adopting ergonomic designs in high schools and local sports clubs, helping drive policy changes and awareness.
